items.title: ‘I was very aggressive. They threw me out of every school’ … Julie Delpy on acting, anger and predatory directors
items.summary:
Thirty years after the roles that made her famous, the star of Three Colours: White and the Before trilogy is busier than ever – as a screenwriter and director. But, she says, a lot of people have tried to keep her down

To listen to Julie Delpy talk about her workload is to feel the need for a nap coming on. She is writing six screenplays at the moment that range from dark comedies to thrillers. “I don’t do monoculture,” she says. If her producer hadn’t reined her in, she would be working on five horror film scripts too.

The actor, writer and director says she doesn’t sleep well – she can sit at her desk for up to 18 hours, writing “until I run out of steam. I know you could think I’m exaggerating. I’m not. If you look at my computer, you will see how bad it is.”

We’re on a video call, Delpy from her home in Los Angeles. She is charming – intense and funny in big black-framed glasses. “I look so weird with this angle on my hair,” she says, of the ceiling light behind her. “Like an angry bald man!”

Continue reading...
items.t: ‘I was very aggressive. They threw me out of every school’ … Julie Delpy on acting, anger and predatory directors

items.title: ‘She was so not regretful about killing her husband’: the Iranian film that shines a light on blood money and retributive justice
items.summary:
The co-director of An Eye for an Eye, Tanaz Eshaghian, reveals how she came to make a documentary about a woman facing the threat of execution from her husband’s family – as sanctioned by sharia law

“Even though I was raised here,” says the Iranian-American film-maker Tanaz Eshaghian from her home in New York, “I was brought up with the understanding that there are things that you do and things that you don’t do.” Take her 2006 autobiographical feature, Love Iranian-American Style, about her experience of dating in her 20s, which was, she says, “about how I was supposed to marry a nice Iranian man and stay a virgin”. But by the time she’d graduated from Brown University in Rhode Island “that ship had sailed”, she laughs.

Since Love Iranian-American Style, she has made equally taboo-breaking documentaries about a women’s prison in Afghanistan (Love Crimes of Kabul, 2011), trans people in Iran (Be Like Others, 2008) and disabled teenagers in Pakistan (As Far As They Can Run, 2022). And with each new project, the duality of her heritage (Eshaghian emigrated to the US not long after the Iranian revolution when she was six) has spurred her to focus eastwards, closer to where she was born. “When you’ve been raised in the west you can see how similar the thinking is,” Eshaghian says of the similarities she’s found there: “the conservative thinking, the place of women, what’s allowed, what’s important”.

Continue reading...
items.t: ‘She was so not regretful about killing her husband’: the Iranian film that shines a light on blood money and retributive justice

items.title: John Wayne’s 119-Minute Western Thriller 'The Searchers' Is a Start-to-Finish Masterpiece
items.summary: Few movies have as long a trail of imitators and influence as 1956’s The Searchers . Based on Alan Le May ’s novel of the same name, it’s a Western film from the Hollywood director most closely associated with the genre, John Ford , starring the face of the Hollywood Western, John Wayne . The movie might have been received somewhat tepidly as a stirring adventure film in its day, but it came to be seen as a foundational text for the New Hollywood school of filmmakers, casting a shadow over movies as diverse as Taxi Driver , Star Wars , and Paris, Texas . As a story of obsession, vengeance, and what it means to live in a society, it struck an uneasy chord for those directors, becoming something of an obsession in itself, and gave John Wayne possibly the darkest role he ever played, with his genial smile and rough monosyllabic manner of speaking twisted by John Ford.
items.t: John Wayne’s 119-Minute Western Thriller 'The Searchers' Is a Start-to-Finish Masterpiece

items.title: The Fox review – talking animals are the least weird thing in this delightfully peculiar comedy
items.summary:
Dario Russo’s debut feature is Brothers Grimm meets Yorgos Lanthimos, with a standout cast including Olivia Colman, Sam Neill and Emily Browning

The vibe of writer-director Dario Russo’s delightfully peculiar feature debut is “messed-up fairytale”, pitched somewhere between the Brothers Grimm and Yorgos Lanthimos, with a distinctly Australian je ne sais quoi.

Russo is perhaps best known for co-creating the spy comedy series Danger 5, which had an aesthetic inspired by 60s and 70s men’s magazines; The Fox has a similarly thick retro texture. I love how this film feels as though it was made in consultation with the animal world, taking place in a universe where animals can speak to humans – though that’s perhaps the least weird thing about it.

items.t: The Fox review – talking animals are the least weird thing in this delightfully peculiar comedy

items.title: 14th review – Ava DuVernay takes on a bully president and his viper’s-nest court of Maga sycophants
items.summary:
DuVernay’s follow-up to her dissection of the 13th Amendment to the US constitution is a vehement and exhilarating defence of democracy

Ava DuVernay’s previous documentary 13th, energised by the Black Lives Matter movement, was a brilliant polemic about the 13th Amendment to the US constitution, which she argued perpetuated a link between slavery and prison for African American men. Ten years later, and after an almost continuous decade of Trumpism, DuVernay has made a follow-up film about the 14th Amendment, and she has evidently arrived at a rather different attitude to the constitution and its authors’ intentions and good faith. Now she sees the enemy as Maga and the constitution as something that must be defended against a tinpot bully president and his viper’s-nest court of sycophants.

The shift in view is not acknowledged, but the overall effect is similar. Utilising a gallery of very smart talking-head interviewees, including conservative Republicans, DuVernay has mounted a vehement and exhilarating defence of what might be called the second American Enlightenment, created by the 13th, 14th and 15th “reconstruction” amendments, drawn up between 1865 and 1870 after the American civil war. The 14th…
items.t: 14th review – Ava DuVernay takes on a bully president and his viper’s-nest court of Maga sycophants

items.title: ‘I said no thanks to the casting couch. But other actresses had problems’: Jane Alexander on 50 years of stardom
items.summary:
The Great White Hope, All the President’s Men, Kramer vs Kramer … Alexander has a CV most actors can only dream of. She talks us through the highs and lows – including a ‘beautiful’ encounter with Muhammad Ali

Jane Alexander will never forget the play that won her a Tony award, a husband and her first film role. The Great White Hope, which ran on Broadway from 1968 to 1970, was based on the life of Black boxer Jack Johnson, who in 1908 became world heavyweight champion in segregated America. Alexander played Eleanor, a white woman married to an African American boxer also called Jack, at a time when interracial marriages were still illegal in many states.

Decades later, when the play opened, the US supreme court had only recently struck down all remaining bans – and Alexander received hate mail and death threats for the role.

Continue reading...
items.t: ‘I said no thanks to the casting couch. But other actresses had problems’: Jane Alexander on 50 years of stardom

items.title: Reeling in the years: how Hollywood fell for its own vanishing glories
items.summary:
The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth is the latest in a growing wave of movies steeped in nostalgia for a heyday in stark contrast to its current ruination

If Los Angeles was a person, it might just be a laid-back fiftysomething trouper with cool sunglasses and an even better haircut. Some dodgy episodes in his past, but still handles himself with style. In other words, Los Angeles personified is Cliff Booth – the over-the-hill stuntman played by Brad Pitt in Once Upon a Time … in Hollywood, now turned studio fixer in the sequel, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.

Set eight years later in 1977, Further Mis-Adventures is more plot-driven, more Elmore Leonard-esque than the pure expansive “memory piece” of Once Upon a Time. But both films are steeped in the ambience and lore of old LA, drawn in part from Quentin Tarantino’s memories of cruising around the streets aged six in his stepdad’s Karmann Ghia (the car Booth also drives). They’re part of the recent intensely nostalgic LA revivalist mini-boom of work that also includes Paul Thomas Anderson’s Licorice Pizza (2021), Damien Chazelle’s Babylon (2022) and Ti West’s
items.t: Reeling in the years: how Hollywood fell for its own vanishing glories

items.title: You Can See Everything passes $100m at global box office as UK release starts strong
items.summary:
The documentary from Nathan Fielder following fraudster Elizabeth Holmes in the weeks leading up to her imprisonment has broken box office records in the UK

Elizabeth Holmes film You Can See Everything has crossed the $100m mark at the global box office as it recorded the highest ever opening weekend figure for a non-music documentary in the UK.

Directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, You Can See Everything earned an estimated $2.5m over the weekend on its sixth week of release in North America, according to Box Office Mojo, bringing its total there to $93.5m. This has been augmented by successful releases in a number of international territories, which has added an estimated $9m for a total of $102.5m.
